questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How soap is made in factories from oils and fats
Riddles and puzzles about everyday objects at home
The history of Hungarian medicine in the 1800s
Why handwashing matters and how to explain it
questions.why: They discuss the importance of handwashing and the lessons from Dr Semmelweiss.

questions.q: What is the answer to Neil's riddle, “so big I'm everywhere but so small you can't see me”?
options: Air
Germs
Your breath
Water
questions.why: Neil says the answer is germs.

questions.q: Why was Dr Ignaz Semmelweiss called the 'saviour of mothers'?
options: He kept maternity wards free of germs
He invented a new medicine for mothers
He built the first children's hospital
He trained thousands of midwives
questions.why: Neil says he was known as the 'saviour of mothers' for keeping maternity wards germ-free.

questions.q: Where has Val Curtis mostly worked to improve hygiene?
options: In London hospitals
In schools in Hungary
In developing countries
In soap factories
questions.why: She says she's spent thirty years trying to improve hygiene, mostly in developing countries.

questions.q: Why does Val Curtis call Semmelweiss her 'patron saint'?
options: He was her teacher at university in London
He was a religious man, and so is she
He saved the lives of people in her family
He inspired her life's work on handwashing
questions.why: She says handwashing has been her life, and he was the first to see the importance of clean hands.

questions.q: What made people start to take handwashing seriously, according to Val Curtis?
options: A 2003 paper showing it could save a million lives
The coronavirus outbreak
A government advertising campaign
The work of Semmelweiss in the 19th century
questions.why: She says it wasn't until their 2003 paper showed it could save a million lives that people took it seriously.

questions.q: What lesson does Val Curtis take from Semmelweiss?
options: Shout loudly so that people finally listen to you
Keep your research secret until it is finished
Share the data patiently and tell your story well
Blame the people who don't wash their hands
questions.why: She says don't scream and shout, but patiently get the data out and tell your story positively.

questions.q: What does Georgina say happens if you scream and shout at people?
options: They change their behaviour quickly
They don't listen and think you're strange
They become angry and shout back
They ask for more evidence
questions.why: She says people don't listen if you scream and shout at them; they just think you're strange.
